## The Cascadia Portfolio {#cascadia-portfolio}

Cascadia is a portfolio built to be checked, not taken on faith. Each module carries its own governance layer — certified measures, frozen baselines, a validation suite that fails the build rather than ship a number I can't defend — so a claim on this site is a claim you can verify against the data behind it, not just read. The stack varies by problem: a governed SQL Server → Microsoft Fabric → Power BI enterprise pipeline, pragmatic local SQL Server + Power BI, lightweight Python → DuckDB/SQLite → static ECharts on real SEC, federal court, and economic data, and the program side of BI — platform migration and metric governance. The through-line isn't the architecture; it's that every number on every page can be tested against its source.

### Cascadia Matter Ledger
<span class="badge-status new">New</span><span class="badge-status">Live</span>

Eleven million public federal civil case records, frozen and hash-verified, modelled into certified legal-operations measures — then a scheduled pipeline that re-asserts its own invariants twice a day, reconciles against the frozen baseline, and publishes the failures. Ask it one ordinary question and the ungoverned answer comes back negative.

### Cascadia Control Tower
<span class="badge-status new">New</span><span class="badge-status">Live</span>

Three fill rates computed from one dataset, all arithmetically correct and 7.0 points apart — and a split-shipment cost that none of them measures. Certifies one definition, prices the leak against a modelled no-split counterfactual, and shows why no single split threshold works across two banners. Synthetic operations, anchored to BLS, Census and SEC data.

### The Combinatorics of Sibling Conflict
<span class="badge-status">Preprint</span>

Not an analytics module — a short mathematics paper. The number of ways n children can take sides against each other, with the rest uninvolved, is (3^n^ − 2·2^n^ + 1)/2, the Stirling number S(n+1, 3). Of the 25 ways four children can, 6 are one against one; of the 3,025 ways eight children can, 28 are.

[Read It](projects/sibling-conflict.qmd){.btn .btn-primary .btn-sm}
[The Paper (PDF)](https://www.robbinsanalytics.com/assets/Robbins-Combinatorics-of-Sibling-Conflict.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-secondary .btn-sm}
